name: Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages
title: Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages
answer: English learners' families and heritage speakers bring language assets that schools should treat as strengths, not deficits. AI can translate messages both ways so parents can help with homework even without strong English, and can generate home-language reading and writing activities at the right level. The point is to keep the home language in the learning, because it supports content learning and makes school more meaningful.

sections.body: This idea is about treating the languages students bring from home as resources for learning rather than obstacles to overcome. Families of English learners are partners in education, and a parent who is not confident in English can still support homework when instructions and tips arrive in the family's own language. Heritage speakers, who grew up speaking a language at home, may be English learners or may speak English well while wanting to build literacy in their home language. AI can help by producing reading and writing activities in that language at the right level. The problem it solves is that schools often operate on monolingual norms, which shut out both families and the language skills students already have.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher can send instructions and homework tips to families in their own language through TalkingPoints, which translates messages in both directions, so a parent can respond and help without strong English. For heritage speakers, the teacher can use AI to build reading and writing activities in the home language matched to the student's level, whether that student is still learning English or already speaks it well and wants to develop home-language literacy. The text does not give separate grade-band examples, so the practice applies across ages. Teachers can also look for culturally responsive materials that reflect students' backgrounds, using library databases and AI tools to find them. Whatever is found this way still needs to be checked for accuracy and respect before it reaches students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one evidence label for this idea. A review of 94 publications found that using students' home languages helped them learn content, and that monolingual norms in schools were a barrier (Moraru, 2025). That is the finding as the book states it, and it supports both the family communication side and the heritage speaker side of the idea. The book does not present additional studies or figures beyond this review. The claim that culturally responsive materials make learning more meaningful is presented as practice rather than as a separate research finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Materials found through library databases and AI tools must be checked for accuracy and respect, so the teacher, not the tool, decides what is good enough to use. Translation through TalkingPoints supports communication, but the relationship with the family and the judgment about what to send remain with the teacher. The text also names monolingual norms in schools as a barrier, which means the risk sits in school culture and habits, not only in individual lessons. Decisions about a student's level, about which language to use for which activity, and about how to treat language skills as an asset stay with people. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text describes practice rather than compliance rules.
